title: Browser Rendering Pipeline
description: Understand the critical rendering path from HTML bytes to pixels, layout thrashing, compositor layers, and how Core Web Vitals map to real user experience.

segments.text: When a browser receives HTML, it doesn't just display it. It runs a multi-stage pipeline that transforms bytes into pixels. Understanding this pipeline is essential for performance optimization — and for understanding why some changes cause 60fps jank while others don't.

First, the browser parses HTML into the DOM tree and CSS into the CSSOM tree. HTML parsing is incremental — the browser can start building the DOM while bytes are still arriving. But CSS is render-blocking: the browser won't paint anything until all CSS is parsed because styles could change any element's appearance.

The DOM and CSSOM combine into the render tree. Only visible elements are included: display none elements are excluded, but visibility hidden elements remain because they still take up space. The render tree represents what will actually appear on screen with computed styles.

Layout, also called reflow, calculates the exact position and size of every element. This is expensive: changing one element's width can cascade to hundreds of children. A full page layout on a complex page can take 10 to 50 milliseconds. That's nearly your entire 16.6-millisecond frame budget gone.

Layout thrashing is the performance killer. Reading a layout property like offsetHeight forces the browser to synchronously recalculate layout. If you read and write in a loop — read offsetHeight, set style.height, repeat — you force layout recalculation on every iteration. I've seen this cause 200-millisecond jank on mobile.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you batch DOM reads and writes to avoid layout thrashing?

segments.text: After layout, the browser paints pixels into layers. Not everything goes into one layer. Elements with transform, opacity, will-change, or position fixed get their own compositor layer. This is critical: changes to a composited layer don't trigger repaint of other layers.

The compositor runs on the GPU and combines layers into the final image. Animations using transform and opacity are compositor-only: they skip layout and paint entirely. This is why translate3d is fast but changing top/left is slow. The GPU handles the math without touching the main thread.

Core Web Vitals map directly to this pipeline. First Contentful Paint measures when the first text or image renders. Largest Contentful Paint tracks when the main content is visible — should be under 2.5 seconds. Cumulative Layout Shift measures unexpected layout shifts that frustrate users.

Layout shifts happen when elements load without reserved dimensions. An image without width and height causes content to jump when it loads. Web fonts cause a flash of unstyled text. Dynamically injected ads push content down. Pinterest reduced CLS by 40 percent by adding aspect-ratio CSS to all image containers.

Optimizing the critical rendering path means reducing what blocks first paint. Inline critical CSS to avoid an extra round trip. Defer non-critical JavaScript with async or defer attributes. Preload fonts with link rel preload. The goal: get the first meaningful paint under one second on 3G.

A real scenario: your React app shows a blank screen for three seconds. Server response is 200 milliseconds. The problem? A 500KB JavaScript bundle that blocks rendering. The browser can't paint until the JS is parsed, compiled, and executed. On a mid-range phone, that's two to three seconds of dead time.
segments.thought_prompt: How would you restructure a 500KB JS bundle to get first paint under one second?

segments.text: The rendering pipeline is your performance budget. Layout costs milliseconds per frame. Paint costs depend on layer complexity. Compositing is nearly free on the GPU. Know which CSS properties trigger which pipeline stages, and you can build interfaces that feel instant even on low-end devices.
